# Analysis of White Dwarf Binary Signals in the Mock LISA Data Challenges

## Overview

This study presents an analysis of selected single source data sets drawn from the first round of the Mock LISA Data Challenges (MLDC), with a specific focus on white dwarf binaries. These challenges provide a valuable framework for developing and testing the data analysis techniques that will be essential for extracting astrophysical signals from future space-based gravitational wave observations.

## Methodology

To address the challenge of detecting and characterizing these signals, the researchers developed and implemented an end-to-end analysis pipeline. This pipeline integrates two complementary components:

- A **grid-based coherent pre-processing unit**, which is responsible for the initial signal detection, and
- An **automatic Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) post-processing unit**, which performs detailed signal evaluation.

By combining these two approaches, the pipeline is designed to leverage the strengths of each method, moving systematically from initial detection through to precise parameter estimation.

## Results

The performance of the pipeline demonstrated several important outcomes. First, the coherent approach employed in the pre-processing stage proved capable of providing secure and accurate signal detection, establishing a reliable foundation for subsequent analysis.

Building upon this initial detection, the Markov Chain Monte Carlo approach further improved the overall detection accuracy. Beyond refining the detection itself, the MCMC routine supplied additional valuable information regarding the signal parameters, offering a more complete characterization of the underlying sources.

Finally, the MCMC routine demonstrated an additional capability: it was able to accurately determine the noise level within the frequency window of interest. This ability to characterize the noise environment alongside the signal parameters represents a significant advantage, as it contributes to a more robust and self-consistent analysis of the data.

## Conclusion

Taken together, these results demonstrate that the combined coherent and MCMC pipeline offers an effective strategy for the detection and characterization of white dwarf binary signals within the MLDC framework, successfully addressing both signal identification and detailed parameter estimation.

# Analysis of Single-Source White Dwarf Binary Data Sets Using a Combined Grid-Based and MCMC Pipeline

## Introduction

The detection and characterization of gravitational wave signals from compact binary systems represents one of the central challenges in space-based gravitational wave astronomy. Among the most numerous sources expected to populate the millihertz frequency band accessible to the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA) are galactic white dwarf binaries. To develop and validate the analysis techniques required for extracting these signals from the complex LISA data stream, the Mock LISA Data Challenges (MLDC) were established as a community-wide effort to provide realistic simulated data sets against which competing methods could be tested.

## Methodology

In this work, we analyzed single-source white dwarf binary data sets drawn from the first round of the Mock LISA Data Challenges. Our analysis employed an end-to-end pipeline designed to address the two principal stages of the signal analysis problem: detection and evaluation.

The first stage of our pipeline consisted of a grid-based coherent pre-processing step dedicated to signal detection. In this phase, the parameter space was systematically explored using a coherent search strategy, in which template waveforms distributed across a carefully constructed grid were correlated with the data. This approach allowed us to identify candidate signals and to establish approximate estimates of their parameters, providing robust initial conditions for the subsequent refinement stage.

The second stage employed an automatic Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) post-processing routine dedicated to signal evaluation. Building upon the candidate detections identified during pre-processing, the MCMC algorithm explored the local parameter space stochastically, drawing samples from the posterior probability distribution. This Bayesian approach enabled a thorough characterization of the source parameters, including their associated uncertainties and any correlations between them.

## Results

The results of our analysis demonstrate that the combined pipeline achieves secure and accurate signal detection. The grid-based coherent pre-processing reliably identified the injected signals, while the MCMC post-processing yielded improved parameter estimation relative to the initial grid-based estimates. By refining the parameter values through stochastic sampling, the pipeline recovered the source characteristics with high fidelity and provided well-defined credible intervals for each parameter.

A particularly noteworthy outcome of our study is that the Markov Chain Monte Carlo routine additionally determined the noise level within the frequency window of interest accurately. Rather than assuming a fixed, known noise spectrum, the algorithm treated the noise as an unknown quantity to be estimated jointly alongside the signal parameters. This capability is especially valuable for realistic data analysis scenarios, where the noise properties are not known a priori and must be inferred directly from the data.

## Conclusion

Taken together, these findings establish that the integration of grid-based coherent detection with automatic MCMC-based evaluation constitutes an effective and reliable strategy for analyzing single-source white dwarf binary signals in LISA data. The demonstrated ability to achieve secure detection, accurate parameter estimation, and simultaneous noise characterization highlights the promise of this end-to-end approach for application to the increasingly complex data sets anticipated in future space-based gravitational wave observations.

# Mock LISA Data Challenges: Preparing for Space-Based Gravitational Wave Astronomy

## Introduction

As the scientific community prepares for the launch of the **Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA)**, one of the most critical steps in ensuring the mission's success lies in the development and analysis of **mock data**. These simulated datasets, produced long before any real signals reach the detector, play an essential role in testing the tools, algorithms, and methodologies that scientists will eventually use to interpret genuine observations.

## What Is LISA?

LISA is a planned space-based gravitational wave observatory, led by the European Space Agency (ESA) with contributions from NASA. Unlike ground-based detectors such as LIGO and Virgo, LISA will consist of three spacecraft arranged in a triangular formation, separated by millions of kilometers. This configuration allows it to detect low-frequency gravitational waves—signals produced by phenomena such as merging supermassive black holes, extreme mass-ratio inspirals, and compact binaries within our own galaxy.

## The Role of Mock Data

Because LISA will operate in an entirely new frequency band, researchers cannot rely on existing observational data to prepare their analysis pipelines. Instead, they generate **mock data**: artificial datasets that mimic what LISA is expected to observe once operational.

These simulated datasets serve several key purposes:

- **Algorithm testing** — Data analysis techniques can be validated against known "injected" signals whose parameters are hidden from the analysts.
- **Instrument characterization** — Mock data helps model detector noise, instrumental artifacts, and other complications.
- **Source separation** — LISA will detect thousands of overlapping signals simultaneously, so researchers must develop methods to disentangle them.

## The Mock LISA Data Challenges

To coordinate these efforts, the community has organized a series of **Mock LISA Data Challenges (MLDCs)**. In these exercises, a group prepares datasets containing simulated gravitational wave signals buried in realistic noise. Participating teams then attempt to recover the hidden sources and estimate their physical parameters, without knowing the "true" answers in advance.

This blind analysis approach provides an honest assessment of how well current techniques perform, revealing strengths, weaknesses, and areas requiring further development. Over successive challenges, the complexity of the mock data has steadily increased, moving closer to the messy, crowded reality that LISA will encounter in space.

## Why This Matters

The value of mock data extends beyond mere technical preparation. By working with realistic simulations, scientists can:

1. Build confidence that real discoveries will be robust and reproducible.
2. Refine global-fit strategies capable of handling millions of overlapping signals.
3. Train the next generation of researchers in advanced data analysis.

## Conclusion

Mock data lies at the heart of LISA's preparation. By simulating the gravitational wave sky and rigorously testing analysis methods, the scientific community ensures that when LISA finally begins collecting real data, the tools and expertise needed to unlock its discoveries will already be in place. In this way, today's simulated datasets are laying the foundation for tomorrow's breakthroughs in gravitational wave astronomy.

# Abstract

The Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA) will detect gravitational waves from tens of millions of galactic white dwarf binaries, the majority of which will form an unresolved stochastic foreground. Extracting the several tens of thousands of individually resolvable sources from this confusion-limited background presents a formidable data analysis challenge, characterized by a high-dimensional parameter space and significant signal overlap. In this work, we present a hierarchical pipeline that combines grid-based coherent detection with Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) parameter estimation to identify and characterize white dwarf binary signals in the Mock LISA Data Challenges (MLDC) datasets. Our approach first employs a coarse coherent search over a template grid in frequency and sky location to rapidly flag candidate sources and provide robust initial estimates of their parameters. These candidates subsequently seed a refined MCMC exploration that recovers the full posterior distributions of the seven-dimensional gravitational-wave parameters, including amplitude, frequency, frequency derivative, sky position, inclination, and polarization. We apply an iterative source-subtraction scheme to mitigate correlations between overlapping signals and to progressively resolve weaker sources buried in the residual. Testing our pipeline on the MLDC Challenge datasets, we successfully recover the injected sources with high accuracy, demonstrating reliable parameter estimation even in frequency bins containing multiple interfering binaries. We assess the completeness and false-alarm properties of the detection stage and quantify the parameter recovery precision against the injected values. Our results indicate that the combination of computationally efficient grid-based detection with the statistical rigor of MCMC sampling offers a scalable and effective strategy for resolving the galactic binary population, providing a practical framework for the global-fit analyses required by the future LISA mission.

We present an end-to-end pipeline for the detection and characterization of gravitational wave (GW) signals from compact binary coalescences, integrating coherent multi-detector pre-processing with Bayesian Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) parameter estimation. The pipeline ingests raw strain data from a network of interferometers and applies a coherent pre-processing stage comprising data whitening, spectral line removal, and glitch mitigation, followed by a coherent network statistic that combines detector responses while accounting for antenna patterns and inter-detector time delays. Candidate events exceeding an adaptive detection threshold are passed to the post-processing module, where an MCMC sampler explores the multidimensional posterior distribution over intrinsic (masses, spins) and extrinsic (sky location, distance, inclination, coalescence time) parameters. The pipeline yields marginalized posterior distributions, credible intervals, and sky localization maps, while propagating calibration and noise uncertainties throughout. We validate performance on simulated signals injected into representative detector noise, demonstrating reliable recovery of source parameters with well-calibrated uncertainty estimates and computational efficiency suitable for low-latency follow-up. The modular architecture supports extension to additional waveform models and detector configurations, providing a flexible framework for current and next-generation GW observatories.

# Abstract

The Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA) will open the millihertz gravitational wave window, presenting unique data analysis challenges arising from the overlapping and long-lived nature of astrophysical sources in this frequency band. In this work, we present a comprehensive evaluation of signal detection and parameter estimation techniques applied to the Mock LISA Data Challenge (MLDC) datasets. These simulated datasets provide a controlled environment in which known injected signals—including galactic binaries, massive black hole binary mergers, and extreme mass ratio inspirals—are embedded within realistic instrumental noise and confusion foregrounds, enabling rigorous assessment of pipeline performance.

We implement a hybrid detection framework combining matched filtering with stochastic template placement and Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling for global fitting of source parameters. Our methodology addresses the source confusion problem through an iterative subtraction scheme that progressively resolves individual signals from the unresolved galactic background. We quantify detection efficiency, false alarm rates, and parameter recovery accuracy across a range of signal-to-noise ratios and source population densities.

Results demonstrate reliable recovery of the majority of injected sources above a signal-to-noise threshold of 8, with sky localization and intrinsic parameters recovered within statistical uncertainties predicted by the Fisher information matrix. We characterize systematic biases introduced by overlapping signals and instrumental noise mismodeling, and we discuss the computational scalability of our approach toward realistic LISA data volumes. These findings validate key aspects of the proposed analysis strategy and highlight remaining challenges for the global-fit paradigm essential to maximizing the scientific yield of the LISA mission.
